# 2 Samuel Chapter 1 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 168v–169r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2SA_001_page_001.jpg, 2SA_001_page_002.jpg

---

## Consensus Translation

**1** And it came to pass after the death of Saul — David had returned from striking the Amalekites — that David stayed in Ziklag for two days.

**2** On the third day, behold, a man came from the camp, from Saul, with his garments torn and earth upon his head. And when he came to David, he fell to the ground and bowed down.

**3** David said to him, "Where do you come from?" He said, "I escaped from the camp of Israel."

**4** David said to him, "What happened? Tell me, please." He said, "The people fled from the battle, and many of the people fell and died, and Saul and Jonathan his son also died."

**5** David said to the young man who brought him word, "How do you know that Saul and Jonathan his son are dead?"

**6** The young man said, "By chance I happened to be on Mount Gilboa, and there was Saul, leaning upon his spear, and the chariots and horsemen were pressing hard upon him.

**7** He turned and saw me, and called out to me. I said, 'Here I am.'

**8** He said to me, 'Who are you?' And I said, 'I am an Amalekite.'

**9** He said to me, 'Stand over me and kill me, for the agony has seized me, but my life is still wholly in me.'

**10** So I stood over him and killed him, for I knew he could not survive after he had fallen. I took the crown from his head and the band from his arm, and I have brought them here to my lord."

**11** Then David seized his garments and tore them, and all the men who were with him did the same.

**12** They mourned and wept and fasted until evening for Saul and for Jonathan his son and for the people of the LORD and for the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword.

**13** David said to the young man who had brought him word, "Where are you from?" He said, "I am the son of a sojourner, an Amalekite."

**14** David said to him, "How is it that you were not afraid to stretch out your hand to destroy the anointed of the LORD?"

**15** Then David called one of the young men and said, "Come forward — strike him down." And he struck him, and he died.

**16** David said to him, "Your blood is upon your own head, for your own mouth testified against you, saying, 'I killed the anointed of the LORD.'"

**17** Then David lamented with this lamentation over Saul and over Jonathan his son.

**18** He ordered that it be taught to the sons of Judah — "The Bow." It is written in the Book of the Upright:

**19** "The glory of Israel is slain upon your heights!
How the mighty have fallen!

**20** Tell it not in Gath,
proclaim it not in the streets of Ashkelon,
lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice,
lest the daughters of the uncircumcised exult.

**21** O mountains of Gilboa,
let there be no dew and no rain upon you, nor fields of offerings!
For there the shield of the mighty was defiled,
the shield of Saul — anointed with oil no more.

**22** From the blood of the slain,
from the fat of the mighty,
the bow of Jonathan did not turn back,
and the sword of Saul did not return empty.

**23** Saul and Jonathan —
beloved and gracious in their lives,
and in their death they were not divided.
Swifter than eagles,
stronger than lions.

**24** O daughters of Israel, weep over Saul,
who clothed you in scarlet with fine things,
who set ornaments of gold upon your garments.

**25** How the mighty have fallen in the midst of battle!
Jonathan lies slain upon your heights!

**26** I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan.
Very dear were you to me.
Your love to me was wonderful,
surpassing the love of women.

**27** How the mighty have fallen,
and the weapons of war have perished!"

---
## SOPHIA's Council Notes

All three translators agree on the narrative structure and sequence of events: the Amalekite messenger's report (vv.1–10), David's mourning and execution of the messenger (vv.11–16), and the Song of the Bow lament (vv.17–27). The poetic structure of the lament — with its tripartite refrain "How the mighty have fallen" (vv.19, 25, 27) — is consistently recognized by all three. The Masoretic text is stable for this chapter, with no major textual variant requiring adjudication.

---
## Disagreement Log

### V.1 — "stayed" vs. "sat" vs. "stayed"
- **EMET:** "David sat in Tsiqlag" (hyper-literal *yeshev*)
- **LOGOS:** "David stayed in Ziklag"
- **PNEUMA:** "stayed in Ziklag"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "stayed in Ziklag." The verb *yashav* means "to sit/dwell/remain." In context, "stayed" (LOGOS/PNEUMA) is more natural than the positional "sat." English conventional spelling "Ziklag" preferred over transliterated "Tsiqlag."

### V.4 — "How did things go?" vs. "What was the word?" vs. "What happened?"
- **EMET:** "What was the word?"
- **LOGOS:** "How did things go?"
- **PNEUMA:** "What happened?"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "What happened? Tell me, please." The Hebrew *mah hayah ha-davar* is literally "what was the word/matter." LOGOS captures the idiomatic sense; PNEUMA is most natural. I adopt the concise "What happened?" while retaining EMET/LOGOS's "Tell me, please" (*nagged-na li*) which PNEUMA omitted.

### V.6 — "by chance I happened" vs. "happening I happened" vs. "I happened to be"
- **EMET:** "Happening I happened upon-mount the-Gilboa" (preserving infinitive absolute)
- **LOGOS:** "By chance I happened to be on Mount Gilboa"
- **PNEUMA:** "I happened to be on Mount Gilboa"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "By chance I happened to be on Mount Gilboa." LOGOS captures the emphatic infinitive absolute (*niqroh niqreti*) with "by chance" while maintaining readability.

### V.6 — "leaning" vs. "slumped"
- **EMET:** "leaning upon his spear"
- **LOGOS:** "leaning upon his spear"
- **PNEUMA:** "slumped on his spear"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "leaning upon his spear." The Hebrew *nish'an* means "leaning/supporting himself." PNEUMA's "slumped" adds interpretive weight not present in the verb. The context already conveys Saul's dire state.

### V.9 — "anguish" vs. "agony" vs. "agony has me in its grip"
- **EMET:** "seized-me the-anguish [shavats]"
- **LOGOS:** "anguish has seized me"
- **PNEUMA:** "the agony has me in its grip"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "the agony has seized me." I adopt "agony" (LOGOS/PNEUMA) as more vivid than "anguish" for the rare *shavats* (death-cramp), and use LOGOS's verbal structure "has seized me" which is closer to the Hebrew syntax.

### V.10 — "bracelet" vs. "band"
- **EMET:** "the-bracelet that [was] upon-his-arm"
- **LOGOS:** "the bracelet that was on his arm"
- **PNEUMA:** "the band from his arm"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "the band from his arm." The Hebrew *ets'adah* refers to an armband or arm-bracelet. "Band" (PNEUMA) is the more accurate term for a royal arm-ornament worn by a warrior-king.

### V.12 — "the people of the LORD" vs. "the LORD's people"
- **EMET:** "the-people of-YHWH"
- **LOGOS:** "the people of the LORD"
- **PNEUMA:** "the LORD's people"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "the people of the LORD" — follows the project convention and the Hebrew construct chain *am YHWH*.

### V.19 — "beauty" vs. "glory" vs. "pride"
- **EMET:** "The-beauty [tsevi]"
- **LOGOS:** "The glory"
- **PNEUMA:** "Your pride"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "The glory of Israel." The Hebrew *ha-tsevi* is genuinely multivalent. LOGOS's "glory" best captures the sense of national honor and splendor in the context of a royal lament, while remaining close to the formal register of the original.

### V.20 — "uncircumcised" vs. "godless"
- **EMET:** "the-uncircumcised"
- **LOGOS:** "the uncircumcised"
- **PNEUMA:** "the godless"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "the uncircumcised." The Hebrew *arelim* specifically means "uncircumcised ones." PNEUMA's "godless" is interpretive; the term is a physical/covenantal marker, not a moral judgment. The literal term should stand.

### V.21 — "was defiled" vs. "dragged through the dirt"
- **EMET:** "was-defiled"
- **LOGOS:** "was defiled"
- **PNEUMA:** "was dragged through the dirt"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "was defiled." The Hebrew *nig'al* means "was polluted/defiled." PNEUMA's rendering adds vivid imagery not in the text. The formal verb "defiled" preserves the ritually-charged language of the original.

### V.21 — "not anointed with oil" vs. "no longer anointed with oil" vs. "never again rubbed with oil"
- **EMET:** "not anointed with-oil"
- **LOGOS:** "no longer anointed with oil"
- **PNEUMA:** "never again rubbed with oil"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "anointed with oil no more." A slight reshaping for poetic rhythm while preserving the meaning. The Hebrew *beli mashiach ba-shamen* is a powerful wordplay: Saul, the *mashiach* (anointed one) of YHWH, now has a shield that is *beli mashiach* (without anointing).

### V.22 — "fat" vs. "flesh"
- **EMET:** "the-fat"
- **LOGOS:** "the fat"
- **PNEUMA:** "the flesh"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "the fat." The Hebrew *chelev* means "fat" specifically. PNEUMA's "flesh" broadens the meaning unnecessarily. The parallelism blood // fat is precise military imagery — the weapons consumed the enemy completely.

### V.23 — "pleasant" vs. "gracious" vs. "full of grace"
- **EMET:** "the-beloved and-the-pleasant"
- **LOGOS:** "beloved and pleasant"
- **PNEUMA:** "loved and full of grace"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "beloved and gracious in their lives." The Hebrew *ha-ne'imim* means "the pleasant/lovely ones." "Gracious" (combining LOGOS's register with PNEUMA's warmth) captures both the personal charm and the noble bearing of the fallen heroes.

### V.26 — "pleasant" vs. "dear"
- **EMET:** "You-were-very pleasant to-me"
- **LOGOS:** "Very pleasant were you to me"
- **PNEUMA:** "How dear you were to me"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "Very dear were you to me." PNEUMA's "dear" better conveys the emotional weight of the Hebrew *na'amta li me'od* in this deeply personal verse, while LOGOS's inverted syntax ("Very... were you") maintains the formality of the qinah.

### V.26 — "wonderful" vs. "a thing of wonder"
- **EMET:** "Wonderful [was]-your-love to-me"
- **LOGOS:** "Your love to me was wonderful"
- **PNEUMA:** "Your love for me was a thing of wonder"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "Your love to me was wonderful." LOGOS's rendering is most accurate — *nifle'atah* is the niphal of פלא (to be extraordinary/wonderful). PNEUMA's expansion adds emphasis not present in the original.

---
*— SOPHIA, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
